source.title: SPARQ: Synthetic Problem Generation for Reasoning via Quality-Diversity Algorithms
source.authors: Alex Havrilla; Edward Hughes; Mikayel Samvelyan; Jacob Abernethy

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream performance under scaling synthetic training data and generator-model size, in a synthetic math-data setting rather than language-model pretraining-loss scaling.
record.gate_note: Reports downstream accuracy and relative improvement, not held-out cross-entropy loss, parameter/token/compute loss laws, or compute-optimal parameter-token allocation. Inference-time sampling results and data-quality/diversity ablations do not test the listed scale-or-pretraining-loss version.
record.test_reason: The study is about synthetic math-problem generation for fine-tuning Gemma-2-9b. It reports downstream MATH and AIME accuracy as fine-tuning data count and problem-generator size grow. It fits no power law, reports no loss, and does not scale the trained model's own parameters, pretraining tokens or compute. The abstract says it 'confirms' model and data scaling laws, but the evidence is a few monotone accuracy gains with no functional form. So its results do not bear on any version as stated. V6 concerns downstream performance against the trained model's scale or pretraining loss. V5 requires the power-law form to hold in fine-tuning. Neither is measured. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SPARQ-generated data gives up to 9% absolute gains over SFT (up to 24% relative, per the abstract). They add that the gains scale with generator size and generated data amount. They also conclude that higher-quality, harder data helps in-distribution performance and more diverse data helps OOD generalization, and that models can self-improve by generating their own problems.
record.recipe_differences: Studies synthetic math-problem generation and downstream fine-tuning accuracy, rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss power laws or finding compute-optimal parameter-token splits.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream outcomes vary with the amount of generated data and generator size. The paper also reports outcome differences by data-generation and filtering strategy, and by inference-sample budget for OOD evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: MATH accuracy of a fine-tuned Gemma-2-9b rises with the number of synthetic generated problems, roughly +1.5% when the count triples (Fig. 2). In Fig. 6 it also rises with the number of filtered training samples N from 2^12 to 2^15, but no functional form is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream accuracy after supervised fine-tuning increases monotonically with the amount of synthetic fine-tuning data.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger problem-generator models yield more useful training problems for a fixed 9B student: a 2B generator gives +5% over baseline, and larger generators add +2.5% and then +1.5% (Fig. 8 right).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The scale of a synthetic-data generator model predicts the downstream gain of a fixed-size student trained on its data.

record.problems: The reported scaling evidence is limited to downstream accuracy in synthetic math-data experiments; the text gives no uncertainty estimates for these results. Some size-scaling increments are not assigned to specific generator sizes in the prose.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. Inference-time compute comparisons and data-quality/diversity filtering ablations are not rows for the tested version because they do not measure performance as a function of model/data scale or pretraining loss as specified by V6.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss and no parameter, token or compute loss scaling.
Fine-tuning data scaling is shown only as monotone gains. No power-law form is fitted or tested.
No variation of the trained model's scale and no relation to pretraining loss. The student is fixed at Gemma-2-9b, apart from the 2B self-improvement run, which reports only relative gain.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 'supports' label is dropped. The scaling axes are fine-tuning data count and generator size, neither of which is what V6 names. r2–r4 are the study's own method compared with its baseline. The paper's 'scaling laws' language is informal: no power-law fit, exponents or loss are reported, and no uncertainty is given.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or training compute.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed training-compute budget allocation between parameters and tokens.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
No test of the same power-law form across modalities or the listed training regimes.
Tests downstream MATH performance with synthetic-data and generator scaling, but not prediction from pretraining loss or broad downstream task coverage.
No fitted exponents, fit-method comparisons, or tests of curve bending in pretraining-loss scaling.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b
rows.operation_detail: Scaled the number of generated problem-solution pairs used for downstream training.

conditions.value: tripling the number of generated problems

rows.locator: Section 3.1, Main Results for Problem Generation
rows.note: The text reports the change with tripled generated-problem count but does not give the compared counts or specify whether the percentage is relative or absolute.
rows.check: Measures fine-tuning data quantity (generated problems) against MATH accuracy: roughly +1.5% for tripling. This is neither model or pretraining scale (V6) nor a fitted power law (V5). The compared counts are not stated in the text and are only visible in Figure 2.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b student trained on static uniform SPARQ data
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on generated synthetic problem-solution data.
rows.locator: Abstract; Section 3.1, Main Results for Problem Generation
rows.note: The paper describes this as an absolute 9% improvement over the SFT baseline.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (SPARQ static uniform data) against the SFT baseline, 38% to 47%. It is a method-performance result, not a scaling result, and should not be a row for this claim.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b
rows.operation_detail: Self-synthetically generated problems and trained on the resulting data.
rows.note: The paper reports the relative improvement after generating 300K problem-solution pairs.
rows.check: Self-improvement of 9B over its own SFT baseline (relative 20%). This is a method gain, not performance as a function of scale.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Self-synthetically generated problems and trained on the resulting data.
rows.note: The paper reports the relative improvement after generating 300K problem-solution pairs.
rows.check: Self-improvement of 2B over its own SFT baseline (relative 15%). This is a method gain. Comparing r3 with r4 contrasts relative gains, not downstream performance with scale.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b student
rows.operation_detail: Varied the size of the problem-generator model and measured student performance.

conditions.value: varied; exact sizes for the stated increments not specified in text

rows.baseline: baseline performance; numeric value not stated
rows.value: A 2B generator gives 5% improvement; scaling the generator adds another 2.5% and 1.5% improvement cumulatively.
rows.note: The prose does not assign the two incremental gains to particular generator sizes.
rows.check: Varies the size of the problem-generator model, not the trained student's (fixed 9B) size. The increments (+5%, then +2.5%, +1.5%) are not assigned to specific sizes in the text, and the baseline is not stated.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported synthetic-data scaling and generator-size comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Downstream performance improves with more generated problems and with generator scaling in the reported settings (r1, r5); the paper also reports gains from self-generated training data relative to SFT baselines (r2-r4).
